question: Tell me about a time you noticed an us-and-them dynamic forming. What did you do to break it down?

raiseTranscript.text: On my first project, the backend team and frontend team started avoiding each other in standups and blaming delays on the other side. I asked my manager if I could set up a quick shared Slack channel and a 15-minute weekly sync just for the two devs on each side. We started sharing small wins there and it reduced the finger-pointing.
The channel stayed active and we caught two integration issues early. My manager later asked me to document the format for the next project.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you noticed an us-and-them dynamic forming. What did you do to break it down?
Role: new grad on first project; noticed backend/frontend blame in standups
Action: asked manager permission, created shared Slack + 15-min weekly sync
Outcome: channel stayed active, caught two issues early; manager asked to document format
Quote: 'We started sharing small wins there and it reduced the finger-pointing.'
Follow-up: What happened after that sync? -> documented for next project
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Break down silos. Junior candidate described an individual-scope action on their first project: requesting permission to create a shared Slack channel and 15-minute sync between backend and frontend. Quote: 'We started sharing small wins there and it reduced the finger-pointing.' The outcome stayed local yet produced measurable early issue detection and the manager asked to reuse the format. Shows ownership of their immediate work and coachability in looping the manager first. Biggest strength: turned a noticed friction into a repeatable micro-process without overstepping scope.

lowerTranscript.text: I saw the two teams not talking much so I just tried to be friendly and say hi in the hallway. It didn't really change anything but at least I wasn't part of the problem.
Did you try anything more structured?
No, I figured it was above my pay grade so I focused on my own tickets.

raiseTranscript.text: Marketing and product started treating each other as blockers on a launch. I pulled the two leads into a room and mapped the actual handoff steps on a whiteboard, then volunteered to run a shared retro after the launch. We ended up creating a joint checklist that both teams adopted.
How did you get the leads to agree?
I framed it as reducing rework for both sides and offered to own the first retro agenda so neither team had extra work upfront.

No, I stayed in my lane and let management handle it.

raiseTranscript.text: Engineering and sales had developed separate roadmaps that conflicted on priorities. I created a quarterly joint planning ritual with shared OKRs and asked both VPs to co-present the first one. After two quarters the org stopped maintaining duplicate plans and we reallocated two headcount to a joint initiative.
What trade-offs did you make to get the VPs aligned?
I accepted that the first quarter would have some overlap and focused the OKRs only on the three highest-conflict areas rather than forcing full alignment immediately.
